item.title: Exit Strategy: Part Smart and Leave People on a High Note
item.description:
Relationships

Exit Strategy: Part Smart and Leave People on a High Note

Communicating closure counts and says a lot about one’s character.

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • Poor exits at work, in relationships, or with habits are often fraught with fear and avoidance.
  • Today we have phrases made popular that glorify the horrible pattern of a cut-and-run parting style.
  • When we don’t part smart, we may repeat similarly poor mistakes in the future.

If first impressions matter, last impressions matter even more. People dread handing in a two- to four-week notice at work. They stay silent when a relationship has struggles rather than communicate, which could mend matters. Poor habits creep into exits, especially with technology, yet bad departures can create a lifetime of disappointment, uneasy questions, and lingering emotion.

Dr. Henry Cloud, author of Necessary Endings: The Employees, Businesses and Relationships That All of Us Have to Give Up in Order to Move Forward, writes, “Endings are a natural part of the universe. Your life and business must face them, stagnate or die.” There’s a universality of endings to get to the next level and grow. Endings you avoid don’t disappear, per Dr. Cloud. They cost more the longer you wait to face them.

Leaving a Job

In our information age, industries are interconnected. News of unprofessional behavior travels among former colleagues and second-hand channels. When flooded with emotion after being let go or pressured to resign, some don’t think about the months that follow. Sabotaging the office, badmouthing others, and unpleasant behavior bodes poorly for that needed LinkedIn endorsement or job reference. You also don’t want to be branded with an internal red flag in HR not to rehire if the trajectory of your path ever changes.

Before you exit, give adequate notice, leave needed records, and be a resource. Maintain positive relationships with colleagues for everyone’s sake because a solid professional network pays off.

Goodbye to a Habit

Kicking a bad habit has health and relationship benefits. If you don’t, other partings may be rendered a moot point. We spend a shocking 43% of our day doing things without thinking, says Wendy Wood in Good Habits, Bad Habits: The Science of Making Positive Changes That Stick. Willpower alone is inadequate to initiate change.

Humans are wired to pay attention to previous pleasure. It’s tough to eradicate a bad habit. Johns Hopkins neuroscientists demonstrated that when people see something associated with a past reward, their brain flushes with dopamine, without realizing it. Past experiences bias our attention. People they studied who better focused on tasks, resisting distraction, appeared to suppress dopamine release.

Getting rid of a bad habit sheds old, dysfunctional patterns and sets you to a new identity. Hospitals and community centers offer smoking cessation help. Group support aids alcohol, drug, gambling, and even shopping abuse.

In therapy, clients can discuss how to write a letter to their habit-driven selves, attach it to paper, and set it free in the wind or ocean to disintegrate into nature. The symbolic act proves to be powerful.

Smart Relationship Partings

The "Golden Rule"—do unto others as you would want done to you—conveniently slips memory, when humans flood with rage or raw emotion. Imbed that simple motto into your relationship behavior.

We have modern terms to describe opposite bad actions: benching, ghosting, slow fading, orbiting, submarining—all forms of cut, hide, and run. If you wouldn’t want to be kept as a backup option, face stonewalled silence, be reduced over time, or surveilled, don’t do that to others. Of course, there are dangerous relationships, where looking out for number one takes priority. In most others, person number two needs to be a priority also.

As Henry Wadsworth Longfellow wrote, “Great is the art of beginning, but greater is the art of ending.” Pick a private place to have the face-to-face conversation. Use “I statements” vs. “you did or didn’t” ones. Be direct, not offering false friendship hopes or pointing out little flaws. Everyone has these.

Instead, give a reason that makes sense, especially if it’s a long-distance relationship or a distinct difference in life trajectory or interests, and offer genuine compliments. Let the person you’re leaving feel a bit upset or cry, but don’t change your resolve just because you can’t handle conflict or tears.

Kindness matters in parting ways to give others a sense of meaning and hope.
Source: ReciteThis.com

Exiting a Marriage

If there ever was a need to do a debrief, it’s this with so much more at stake here, particularly the longer you’ve been married. Proper closure affords dignity and helps both parties into a next chapter.

Sadly, separations and divorce actions can erupt after years of buildup, with a spark and explosions or implosions—three of four anger stages I wrote about in Overcoming Passive Aggression: How to Stop Hidden Anger from Spoiling Your Relationships, Career and Happiness.

I covered passive aggressive divorce before, but compassion, kindness, and cooperation will help you both move on and have more to show for it (with your finances and character intact). That keeps motive and outcome (discussed in my book) in proper check. With difficult personality traits or a poor marriage genogram that modeled bad exits, poor parting often overrides the will for smart parting.

Frequently, one partner has time to conjure a world on his/her own. Allow the other to catch up emotionally and logistically to figure out reasonable next steps. Impatience on your end doesn’t count as kindness. Certainly, desertion and dumping a host of responsibilities that should be shared is flat-out cruel. Should severing communications without closure ever enter your mind, keep Longfellow’s advice in mind, as that would be equally heartless.

Ambiguous Loss

When there’s no understanding, no post-mortem, maybe even abandonment, ambiguous loss sets in as you grieve a person who is still alive, sometimes one who passes. You’re left with lingering questions and loose ends. Ambiguous loss occurs if there’s a sudden injury rendering a partner in a chronic state that’s severely altered them, or if you suddenly find a secret life or plans to desert you.

Stephanie Sarazin wrote Soul Broken: A Guidebook for Your Journey Through Ambiguous Grief, wherein she tackles caregiver grief to discovering secrets and abandonment. She walks readers through being shell-shocked with anxiety, depression, and self-esteem to work on. Landmines of birthdays, anniversaries, and holidays are triggers. In my own therapy practice and life, I’ve found that rewriting some memories—going to favorite places and dealing with calendar dates, to form fresh ones—helps to balance and respect the past yet move beyond to claim what’s ahead for your own intentions and purposes.

“When we fail to end things well, we are destined to repeat the mistakes that keep us from moving on. We choose the same kind of dysfunctional person or demoralizing job again,” writes Dr. Cloud. “Learning how to do an ending well and how to metabolize the experience allows us to move beyond patterns of behavior that have tripped us up in the past.”

item.title: Could a Weight Loss Medicine Also Protect You From Dementia?
item.description:
Dementia

Could a Weight Loss Medicine Also Protect You From Dementia?

Why dementia prevention—not reversal—remains our best treatment.

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • Dementia is a common late-life disease with few treatments and devastating consequences.
  • There are two distinct approaches to dementia: prevention and treating established disease.
  • Current evidence is equivocal regarding treatment but stronger for prevention.

Sandra spends most Tuesday afternoons in a neurologist's waiting room, scrolling on her phone while her mother finishes a cognitive assessment down the hall. Her mother was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease two years ago, and Sandra has spent those two years learning a hard truth: unlike most of the health crises she has faced in her family, this one comes with few good treatment options and a daunting road ahead.

Sandra is 52. Alzheimer's runs in her family, and she has started to wonder, privately in years past and then more overtly during the past two years, what her own future holds.

Like millions of people struggling with a parent's dementia diagnosis, Sandra has seen the headlines. GLP-1 medicines, the same drugs reshaping conversations about weight and diabetes, are now being discussed as a possible treatment for Alzheimer's disease. She brought the question to her mother's neurologist, Dr. Reyes, hoping for a reason to be optimistic.

Dr. Reyes was careful. The evidence, she explained, is not yet strong enough to recommend a GLP-1 medicine as a treatment for Sandra's mother. The research is real, but premature, and the results so far have been mixed.

Then Dr. Reyes said something Sandra didn't expect. Given Sandra's family history, and that Sandra had already been considering a GLP-1 medicine for other conditions, the more promising conversation was not about treating her mother's disease, but about possibly lowering her own risk.

That distinction, between treating dementia and preventing it, turns out to be the most important thing to understand about this fast-moving area of research.

Why Treatment Remains Uncertain

The excitement about GLP-1 medicines and Alzheimer's disease is substantial, but so is the uncertainty. In late 2025, the two largest clinical trials ever conducted on a GLP-1 medicine and Alzheimer's, testing semaglutide in people who already had mild cognitive impairment, failed to show that the drug slowed the disease's progression.1 Around the same time, a separate and smaller trial of a related medicine, liraglutide, found the opposite: meaningfully less brain volume loss and slower cognitive decline in the treated group.2

Three well-designed studies, contradictory results. That is not a reason for despair, but it is the reason a physicians like Dr. Reyes aren't recommending these medicines as an Alzheimer's treatment. A major new trial, backed by a $100 million investment from the Alzheimer's Association, is now underway specifically to help resolve the contradiction.3

Source: Thomas Rutledge/PowerPoint

The More Promising Story Is Prevention

While the treatment evidence remains unsettled, a separate body of research has been building: not about reversing dementia once it has started, but about whether GLP-1 medicines might lower the chances of it developing in the first place.

This research comes with the major caveat that it observational. Rather than testing the medicine directly against a placebo in a randomized trial, researchers tracked groups of people already taking GLP-1 medicines for diabetes or weight loss, and compared their rates of developing dementia against similar people who were not.

A persuasive pattern emerged (see above "Science Corner"). A 2024 analysis of more than 1 million patients with type 2 diabetes found a 70% lower rate of Alzheimer's diagnosis among semaglutide users compared to those on insulin. A large 2025 study led by Cleveland Clinic researchers, drawing on two separate medical databases, found a significantly reduced Alzheimer's risk associated with starting a GLP-1 medicine. A propensity-matched study of nearly 300,000 patients found a comparable 70% relative reduction in dementia risk. And a 2025 study published in the Annals of Internal Medicine used a research design called target trial emulation, built specifically to approximate what a randomized trial would show using real-world data, and still found a protective association.4-8

The biological reasoning behind these findings is sound. Insulin resistance, chronic inflammation, and poor vascular health are all established contributors to how dementia develops in the brain, and all three are pathways that GLP-1 medicines are known to improve. A medicine that helps regulate blood sugar, reduce inflammation, and support healthy blood vessels is, at least in theory, doing exactly the kind of work that might help protect brain health over time.

"Weighing" the Evidence

It's worth being precise about what these studies can and cannot tell us. Observational research is useful, but it cannot fully rule out other explanations. People who start and stay on a GLP-1 medicine may simply be healthier, more engaged with their medical care, or different in other ways from people who don't. Any of those differences could partly explain the pattern.

That is why the finding from one study is noteworthy: dementia risk did not differ between groups when researchers looked at everyone who started the medicine, but it dropped by 21 percent specifically among people who stayed on it continuously over several years.8 That kind of detail, a benefit tied to sustained use rather than simply filling a prescription, is the sort of pattern that makes a biological effect more plausible than a statistical coincidence.

A Personalized Conversation to Consider

For someone who already has reasons to consider a GLP-1 medicine, family history of dementia, a personal health goal around weight or diabetes management, this research offers something worth discussing directly with a physician: not a promise, but an evidence-backed reason for additional hope.

For someone without another medical reason to take these medicines, the current evidence does not yet support starting one for brain health alone. That may change as the ongoing trials report their results, but it would be getting ahead of the science to act on that basis today.

Sandra left her mother's appointment that Tuesday with the same uncertainty she came in with about her mother's prognosis. But she left with something else too: a specific, doctor-endorsed reason to schedule a different appointment, with her own physician, to ask a question she had not thought to ask before.
